chapter: Opinions on players and ensemble jazz
title: Raymond Burke recordings and Jim Kweskin session; Armand Hug... Naki Parker on piano
summary: Rose recalls an unsuccessful session with Jim Kweskin featuring Burke, then praises pianist Knocky Parker's knowledge, taste and ragtime playing.

That's right, exactly. And prefer to for that matter. Of course I've recorded Rayman a lot. I had that awful session with Jim Queskin, the jug band musician, a couple of years ago. I never had a chance to hear that for some reason. Well, you haven't missed anything, because this man just is not of the talent caliber to go with the kind of a band that we put together for him. And that was supposed to be released on Warner Brothers, but I doubt whether it was good enough. Not that the jazz men weren't, but certainly the records themselves were not good enough, except for the one jambalaya, which just the band played and he didn't participate in. Of course, Rayman was fabulous on that session. One guy can run a session. Oh, of course, especially when he's the lead singer. Does he play an instrument? Yeah, he plays a guitar. He's all right. He's not a bad guitar player, but what I mean is that when you start putting them together in duets with Emmanuel Sales, that the contrast is marked and he's just not up to that caliber. And it needs just an extremely high-quality musician to be able to play with somebody like Sales. Yeah. What about Naki Parker? How do you fit him into that? Well, Naki Parker is a real musical phenomenon. He is a piano player that gives you an enormous feeling of security when he's working on a session for you. In the first place, his knowledge of material is vast, and his taste is good. He always knows the chords, he always knows the appropriate chords, he's always got a lot of original chords to play, which are original without being outlandish. And he never throws the musicians off, he keeps a good beat, and he's really a superb jazz piano player. I'm delighted with him. I'm also delighted with his interpretive capacity on the ragtime pieces that he does, even though he has his weaknesses because he doesn't practice as much as he ought to. But I really feel that he gets the kind of emotional quality into the rags that they were meant to have. And although I can't demonstrate that, I find that it has a very satisfying quality. His playing has a satisfying quality. How do you know he doesn't practice in that? Does he tell you? Are you lying about that? Well, he tells me, and besides that, you know, I have been with Naki at times when I know for a fact that he hasn't played for several days, and he'll go right on a concert without even warming up and sit right down at the piano and start to play.
